Disease relationship: Sjogren disease, SLE, autoimmune cytopenias, autoimmune hepatitis; BAFF-R supports mature autoreactive B-cell survival.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Ianalumab/VAY736 anti-BAFF-R in clinical development; no broad approved BAFF-R antibody confirmed.
Antibody MoA: Antagonism plus possible B-cell depletion depending on Fc design.
Safety concerns: Infection, hypogammaglobulinemia, vaccine response impairment, B-cell depletion toxicity.
Differentiation hypothesis: More selective than soluble BAFF neutralization; may spare APRIL/BCMA plasma-cell biology while removing BAFF-dependent autoreactive B cells.

Location class: Membrane and soluble ligand on activated T cells/platelets
Disease relationship: T-B cell costimulation implicated in SLE, Sjogren disease, MS, transplant and other autoimmune diseases.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Dapirolizumab pegol, frexalimab, dazodalibep and other CD40L blockers in clinical development; historical anti-CD40L programs had thrombotic concerns.
Antibody MoA: Ligand blockade to suppress T-cell help to B cells and antigen-presenting-cell activation; Fc-silent or engineered formats preferred.
Safety concerns: Thrombosis/platelet biology, infection, broad immune suppression.
Differentiation hypothesis: Safer next-generation Fc-silent/fragment formats could revisit a strongly causal immunology node with biomarker-rich B-cell diseases.

Disease relationship: Autoantibody-mediated diseases including gMG, pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, ITP, possibly Sjogren/SLE subsets.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab and others approved or advanced in autoimmune indications.
Antibody MoA: Block IgG recycling to lower pathogenic IgG without direct B-cell depletion.
Safety concerns: Infections, hypo-IgG, albumin/PK effects depending molecule, rebound after discontinuation.
Differentiation hypothesis: Could be differentiated by dosing convenience, depth/duration of IgG lowering, albumin sparing, or disease-specific biomarker selection; target itself is crowded.

Location class: Membrane protein on B cells and plasmablasts
Disease relationship: IgG4-RD, SLE, Sjogren disease, NMOSD and other antibody-driven autoimmune diseases.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Inebilizumab approved for NMOSD and IgG4-RD; obexelimab targets CD19 plus Fc gamma RIIb in development.
Antibody MoA: B-cell/plasmablast depletion or inhibitory co-ligation depending format.
Safety concerns: Infection, hypogammaglobulinemia, prolonged B-cell depletion, PML warning context for B-cell depletion.
Differentiation hypothesis: Non-depleting inhibitory bispecific/co-ligation could improve safety versus depletion in chronic autoimmune diseases.

Disease relationship: AAV, pemphigus, RA, MS, SLE subsets, IgG4-RD; B-cell depletion is clinically validated.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Rituximab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab and biosimilars/related drugs approved across autoimmune/oncology settings.
Antibody MoA: B-cell depletion via ADCC/CDC/apoptosis.
Safety concerns: Infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, infusion reactions, HBV reactivation, PML rare.
Differentiation hypothesis: Very validated but crowded; differentiation would need tissue-selective, safer, or less-depleting design.

Disease relationship: SLE/LN and Sjogren disease B-cell activation; elevated BAFF can promote autoreactive B-cell survival.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Belimumab approved for SLE/LN; blisibimod and other BAFF inhibitors studied.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize soluble/membrane BAFF to reduce B-cell survival signals.
Safety concerns: Infection, depression/suicidality label context, reduced humoral immunity, slow onset.
Differentiation hypothesis: Still useful as benchmark; new seed would need better patient selection or dual pathway design.

Location class: Secreted TNF-family cytokine, can bind proteoglycans
Disease relationship: B-cell/plasma-cell survival, IgA/autoantibody biology; relevant to SLE, IgA nephropathy, Sjogren-like B-cell disease.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Atacicept and telitacicept block BAFF/APRIL; anti-APRIL agents active in kidney/autoimmune pipelines.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize APRIL or dual BAFF/APRIL axis to reduce plasma-cell support.
Safety concerns: Hypogammaglobulinemia, infections, broader antibody suppression than BAFF alone.
Differentiation hypothesis: Differentiation may come from APRIL-selective plasma-cell modulation in autoantibody-high disease.

Disease relationship: Binds BAFF/APRIL; involved in B-cell differentiation and immunoglobulin production; CVID genetics underscore immune role.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Telitacicept/atacicept are receptor-Fc ligand traps, not TACI agonist antibodies; direct TACI-targeting in autoimmunity is less established.
Antibody MoA: Antagonism or inhibitory receptor modulation; alternative is ligand trapping.
Safety concerns: Immunodeficiency-like effects, infection, unpredictable agonism/antagonism biology.
Differentiation hypothesis: Potential to tune B-cell/plasmablast biology differently from BAFF-only blockade, but biology is complex.

Location class: Membrane receptor with soluble receptor form
Disease relationship: RA, giant cell arteritis, systemic sclerosis-ILD, cytokine-driven autoimmune inflammation.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Tocilizumab and sarilumab approved in inflammatory diseases; multiple biosimilars/competitors.
Antibody MoA: Block IL-6 signaling through membrane and soluble receptor pathways.
Safety concerns: Infection, neutropenia, liver enzymes, lipid changes, GI perforation risk.
Differentiation hypothesis: Validated but crowded; differentiation in SSc/rare autoimmune disease would require patient selection and better safety/convenience.

Disease relationship: Broad inflammatory cytokine in RA, AAV, SSc, GCA and cytokine storm-like states.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Siltuximab approved in Castleman disease; IL-6/IL-6R axis widely drugged.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize circulating IL-6.
Safety concerns: Similar IL-6 pathway risks; broad immune suppression.
Differentiation hypothesis: Ligand targeting may differ from receptor blockade but autoimmune space is crowded and differentiation weak.

Location class: Membrane type I interferon receptor chain
Disease relationship: Type I IFN signature in SLE, dermatomyositis, Sjogren subsets and interferonopathies.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Anifrolumab approved for SLE; studied in related autoimmune diseases.
Antibody MoA: Block type I IFN receptor signaling.
Safety concerns: Viral infections, herpes zoster, possible impaired antiviral immunity.
Differentiation hypothesis: Biomarker-high disease selection is attractive; target is validated but SLE differentiation is crowded.

Location class: Membrane C-type lectin on plasmacytoid dendritic cells
Disease relationship: pDC-derived type I IFN in SLE, cutaneous lupus, dermatomyositis/Sjogren-like IFN-high diseases.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Lit-ifilimab/BIIB059 anti-BDCA2 in clinical development for lupus/cutaneous lupus.
Antibody MoA: pDC modulation and reduction of type I IFN production, potentially via receptor engagement/internalization.
Safety concerns: Infection/antiviral immunity, pDC biology uncertainty, injection reactions.
Differentiation hypothesis: Cell-selective IFN pathway modulation may be safer/narrower than IFNAR blockade in IFN-high cutaneous/systemic disease.

Disease relationship: Neutrophilic and epithelial inflammatory skin disease; potential HS, pustular psoriasis, autoimmune blistering/inflammatory skin subsets.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Spesolimab anti-IL-36R approved for generalized pustular psoriasis flares; other IL-36R blockers in development.
Antibody MoA: Block IL-36 cytokine signaling and epithelial-neutrophil inflammation.
Safety concerns: Infections, unknown long-term immune effects, disease selection risk outside pustular psoriasis.
Differentiation hypothesis: Differentiation opportunity in HS or neutrophilic autoimmune skin subsets if biomarker-high IL-36 signature is used.

Disease relationship: Skin inflammation, itch, fibrosis and tissue remodeling; possible HS, prurigo, atopic/type 2 overlap, systemic sclerosis fibrosis hypothesis.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Vixarelimab anti-OSMR in clinical development for prurigo nodularis/atopic dermatitis; autoimmune use less established.
Antibody MoA: Block OSM/IL-31-family receptor signaling depending epitope; reduce inflammation, itch, tissue remodeling.
Safety concerns: Infection unknown, epithelial repair/wound healing effects, receptor biology complexity.
Differentiation hypothesis: Could target chronic inflammatory remodeling rather than only upstream cytokines, useful where scarring/fibrosis drives residual disease.

Disease relationship: IL-6 family cytokine linked to chronic inflammation, stromal activation, fibrosis, IBD/skin inflammatory signatures.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Anti-OSM agents have been clinically explored; no major autoimmune approval confirmed.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize OSM ligand to reduce stromal/fibrotic inflammatory signaling.
Safety concerns: Tissue repair effects, infection/inflammation balance, incomplete pathway blockade through receptor redundancy.
Differentiation hypothesis: Ligand blockade may be cleaner than receptor blockade if OSM-specific signature predicts response.

Disease relationship: Eosinophil/CCR3 chemokine; implicated in fibrosis/inflammation including systemic sclerosis and liver/fibrotic disease hypotheses.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: CM-101/anti-CCL24 reported in clinical development for fibrotic/inflammatory diseases.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize CCL24 to reduce eosinophil/myeloid recruitment and fibrotic signaling.
Safety concerns: Host defense/allergic biology, uncertain causal role, biomarker selection unclear.
Differentiation hypothesis: Relatively less crowded; could differentiate in fibrotic autoimmune subsets where CCL24 is elevated.

Disease relationship: Celiac disease, refractory celiac disease, alopecia/skin autoimmunity and lymphocyte activation biology.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: No approved IL-15RA antibody in autoimmune disease confirmed; IL-15 pathway agents have been clinically tested.
Antibody MoA: Block IL-15 trans-presentation to pathogenic cytotoxic/T/NK cells.
Safety concerns: Infection, NK/T-cell suppression, malignancy surveillance concerns.
Differentiation hypothesis: Strong mechanistic fit in refractory celiac or tissue-resident cytotoxic lymphocyte disease if local biomarkers enrich patients.

Location class: Secreted cytokine, often presented by IL15RA
Disease relationship: Tissue-resident cytotoxic lymphocyte activation in celiac disease, inflammatory skin/muscle autoimmunity hypotheses.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: AMG 714/anti-IL-15 tested in celiac and other inflammatory settings; no broad autoimmune approval confirmed.
Antibody MoA: Neutralize IL-15 to suppress pathogenic cytotoxic lymphocyte activation.
Safety concerns: Infection, NK/T-cell suppression, uncertain efficacy history.
Differentiation hypothesis: Patient selection and local tissue pharmacodynamics would be needed to revive the pathway.

Location class: Secreted complement protein cleaved to C5a/C5b
Disease relationship: AAV, dermatomyositis/complement-mediated injury, NMOSD, autoimmune blistering, thrombotic microangiopathy-like disease.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Eculizumab/ravulizumab approved in complement diseases; vilobelimab anti-C5a authorized/approved in specific inflammatory contexts.
Antibody MoA: Block C5 cleavage or neutralize C5a to reduce terminal complement and/or neutrophil activation.
Safety concerns: Meningococcal and encapsulated bacterial infection, vaccination/prophylaxis burden, high cost.
Differentiation hypothesis: Validated but crowded; disease-specific C5a-sparing or tissue-targeted complement inhibition could differentiate.

Disease relationship: Type 2 inflammation in atopic dermatitis, bullous pemphigoid, prurigo, eosinophilic autoimmune-like skin disease.
Existing drugs / clinical agents: Dupilumab approved across type 2 diseases; investigated/used in bullous pemphigoid contexts.
Antibody MoA: Block IL-4/IL-13 signaling to reduce type 2 inflammation, itch, eosinophilic tissue responses.
Safety concerns: Conjunctivitis, eosinophilia, helminth immunity concerns, target crowding.
Differentiation hypothesis: Useful comparator; new antibody would need BP-specific positioning or differentiated pathway breadth.
